title: A City Gave Black Families $25,000. Now the Government Is Suing.
summary:
Imagine your city did something wrong a long time ago. It made a law that kept Black families from living in certain neighborhoods. That's what happened in Evanston, Illinois, a city near Chicago. In 1921, the city passed a law that pushed Black people into one small area. Banks there wouldn't give them loans to buy homes. That made it hard for Black families to build wealth.

So in 2021, Evanston started a program to say sorry and help. It gave $25,000 grants to more than 300 Black people. Allie Zemtseff used her grant to fix up her kitchen. "It was like they were trying to make amends," she said. Kimberly Holmes-Ross is using her money to turn her basement into an apartment for her son.

But now, the Trump administration is trying to stop the program. The Justice Department joined a lawsuit saying it's unfair because only Black people can get the money. They say it violates the Constitution's equal protection clause, which says the government can't treat people differently because of race. Harmeet Dhillon, a Justice Department official, said, "It is race discrimination, pure and simple."

Supporters say the program is about fixing specific harm. "What's happening in Evanston is the most important civil rights story that no one has heard of," said Alvin Tillery, a professor at Northwestern University. The fight is headed to court.
why_it_matters: It shows that even promises to fix old unfairness can end up in court, and what counts as fair gets decided by people arguing in public — something you'll see in your own community too.

background_read: Evanston, Illinois (a city just north of Chicago), started its program in 2021, and it was one of the first cities in the United States to pay back Black residents for unfair treatment in the past.
For many years, many American cities had rules that kept Black families out of certain neighborhoods, and banks often refused to give them home loans — a practice known as redlining.
Paying people back for harm done long ago has a name: reparations.
Article_Structure: WHO: The city of Evanston, Illinois gave $25,000 grants to more than 300 Black people, while the Trump administration's Justice Department joined a lawsuit to stop the program.
WHAT: A city program meant to make amends for a 1921 law and old bank loan refusals is now being challenged in court as race discrimination.
WHERE: Evanston, Illinois, a city near Chicago, with the fight now headed to court.
WHY: Supporters say the program fixes specific harm from the past, but the Justice Department says it violates the Constitution's equal protection clause because only Black people can get the money.

perspectives.description: They say Evanston's law and bank rules caused real harm to Black families, so giving grants is a way to make amends and help people build wealth.
It says the program is unfair because only Black people can receive the money, and that this is race discrimination and breaks the equal protection clause.
They note that America has argued about reparations for a long time, and judges — not city leaders — may end up deciding whether this kind of program is allowed.
